1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks the e5 pawn at once, aiming to win it back through pressure and quick development rather than by offering more material. Black accepts a pawn deficit for activity while White has to defend a pawn far from his other pieces.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 d6.strategy: Offers a second pawn: after White takes on d6, Black recaptures with the bishop and gets open lines and quick development at the cost of material. White should stay ahead with careful, unhurried play but must watch for attacking tricks.
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 d6.name: Englund Gambit: Hartlaub-Charlick Gambit
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 d6.background: Claude Bloodgood published a book on the gambit in 1998, Blackburne-Hartlaub Gambit, presenting theory he compiled during his prison sentence.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 f6.strategy: Attacks e5 with a pawn to open lines and develop with tempo for the pawn given. The move weakens the kingside, and White can answer by ignoring the offer and building a strong centre, keeping a clear edge.
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 f6.name: Englund Gambit: Soller Gambit

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Qh4.strategy: Brings the queen out at once, eyeing f2, but nothing supports it: White chases it with a developing move such as Nf3 or g3 and keeps the extra pawn. Black has lost time as well as a pawn.
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Qh4.name: Englund Gambit: Mosquito Gambit

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Defends the pawn with a developing move, the simplest way to keep the extra material. The knight is ideally placed on f3, and White can finish development in peace; the only challenge is to see the tactical tricks Black's quick development sets.
